claims.text: Spark plasma sintering enables refractory high-entropy alloy powders to be sintered at lower temperatures than conventional sintering.
Rapid, electrically assisted heating and applied pressure enhance diffusion and densification at lower temperatures.
Refractory high-entropy alloy precursors have high melting points.
Powdered refractory high-entropy alloy precursors have inherent porosity.
A refractory high-entropy alloy can be processed at a sintering temperature around 1200 °C.
The approximately 1200 °C treatment is lower than the temperature required by conventional furnace sintering.
SPS is conducted under vacuum or an inert atmosphere with applied pressure and pulsed electric current.
SPS provides a rapid heating rate.
SPS enhances diffusion along powder-particle interfaces.
Localized Joule heating during SPS promotes neck formation between particles.
Pulsed electric current and applied pressure lower the activation energy for particle bonding and densification.
The SPS mechanism reduces the required sintering temperature.
SPS minimizes grain growth while producing dense microstructures.
Lower-temperature SPS will produce adequate densification and reduced residual porosity.
Lower-temperature SPS will preserve a finer microstructure than conventional higher-temperature sintering.
Conventional furnace sintering or vacuum hot pressing requires higher temperatures to achieve similar densification and phase formation.
The temperature-reduction benefit of SPS is most pronounced for high-melting-point refractory alloys.
The effectiveness of SPS depends on powder particle size, initial oxide content, and processing parameters.
The SPS benefit may be less significant when powder morphology or composition is unsuitable for electrical conduction.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome expects lower-temperature SPS to yield density, porosity, and microstructure comparable or superior to higher-temperature furnace sintering, but the falsification rule treats similar density, porosity, and microstructure as evidence against the hypothesis. Comparable densification at a lower temperature would instead support the central claim.
